beyond_this_part.finding: The source twice prints Tsunao's given name with the steel character 鋼雄 for 綱雄 at p77-p78.
beyond_this_part.why: The English should keep the normalised 'Tsunao', but the house should check the 1895 text rather than treat the normalisation as silently settled.

beyond_this_part.finding: Nothing in this part requires an earlier part to be re-read differently.
beyond_this_part.why: The name variant above is the only cross-part matter raised.

declined.reason: No change to the English name: 'Tsunao' stays as throughout the part, but the 鋼雄/綱雄 variant is not silently normalised — it is flagged below for the editor to check against the 1895 text.

Declined: turning the last line into 'Tomorrow — whose —' makes English syntax, rather than the unstated fate, do the withholding; the present 'Tomorrow, upon whom shall it fall' leaves what falls and upon whom exactly as unnamed as the Japanese does. See the disagreement entry — this one goes up.

The 'bold, decorative pine silhouettes' explanation is declined: the annotated realia get one gloss in the margin, and an inline explanation here would clarify what the sentence itself can carry as 'Kōrin-style shadows'; the hanging 'between' was fixed without it.

'Child's play — as easy as breakfast before morning rice' is declined as an explanatory expansion of 朝飯前; the brisk Japanese idiom is kept visible as 'as easy as breakfast' in Tatsuya's soliloquy, with only the missing hyphen in 'self-satisfied' supplied.

'Newly-hatched chick' and 'clip her wings' are declined as a smoothing of the Japanese bird figure; 'peeping chick' is kept and the technical 'pinion her' replaced by 'her wings are pinned', so the contempt and the one-blow capture remain.

Declined in the suggested form: it punctuates Zenpei's orders with em dashes, which the house uses only where the Japanese has ――; the run of orders, the repeated calling of Mitsuyo and the storehouse detail are the bustle of the scene and are left as one breathless speech rather than re-pointed into separate addressed commands.

Declined: Zenpei's 'What, you say that … is also due?' is his incredulous echo of Tatsuya's terms back at him in negotiation, and recasting it as a clean direct question tidies the airless procedural back-and-forth the reading asks to keep concrete and slightly airless.

Declined as a change, because the present closing lines already keep the fragments as fragments and the pronoun's referent unstated; re-pointing 'above' to 'over' and adding a dash would be rhythm for its own sake on the story's final, deliberately unresolved line.

disagreements.choice: Both taken together in one edit: the beauty is Mitsuyo's alone, and the inward repetition is 'to himself'.
disagreements.faithful_side: F1: 国色 refers to the daughter alone, so the plural 'first beauties of the land' misattributes it to father and daughter both.
disagreements.readable_side: R9: 'repeated in his breast' is not idiomatic English for thinking to oneself.

disagreements.choice: Readable side, in the smallest form: 'shall I laugh in lies, lies, lies?'
disagreements.faithful_side: The wordplay depends on the unvaried echo — Mitsuyo's sixfold 'truly' answered by Zenpei's threefold 'lies' — and the repetition must not be varied or expanded for elegance.
disagreements.readable_side: R12: English cannot 'laugh lies'; the verb needs an object it can govern without losing the mocking parallel.

disagreements.choice: Kept the Japanese idiom visible: 'as easy as breakfast', hyphen only.
disagreements.faithful_side: 朝飯前 is Tatsuya's own brisk sporting idiom in soliloquy; replacing it with plain 'child's play' would flatten the coarse, exuberant ore register the reading requires.
disagreements.readable_side: R14: 'as easy as breakfast' alone is a calque no English reader will hear as an idiom of ease.

disagreements.choice: Present text stands: 'Tomorrow, upon whom shall it fall.'
disagreements.faithful_side: F5: 明日は誰が身の is a fragment the narrator leaves hanging, and supplying 'fall' completes what the Japanese withholds.
disagreements.readable_side: R20: a bare English fragment reads as dropped words rather than deliberate withholding; the line needs a verb's rhythm while 'it' stays unstated.

disagreements.choice: English keeps 'Tsunao' throughout; the variant is flagged rather than represented or silently absorbed.
disagreements.faithful_side: F4: the source's 鋼雄 at p77-p78 differs from 綱雄 elsewhere and should not be silently normalised without checking the 1895 printing.
disagreements.readable_side: No readable note on this span; the English reader is served by one consistent name form.

data.say:
Every other note (F1-F3, R1-R3, R5-R11, R13, R16, R17, and the non-gloss parts of R4, R14 and R15) was taken by edit, in the smallest form that did the job, for the reasons given with each edit in the margin.

Declined, with reasons a reader can follow:
- F5 — see the p132 disagreement below; the fragment question is not settled by declining alone.
- R4's parenthetical explanation of Kōrin, R14's 'child's play — as easy as breakfast before morning rice', and R15's 'newly-hatched chick / clip her wings': each would clarify or smooth an image the Japanese leaves as it stands (a style-word, a soliloquy idiom, a bird figure), so only the grammar around those images was changed.
- R18 — its em-dash re-pointing of Zenpei's orders is declined because the house uses an em dash only where the Japanese has ――; the run-together orders and repeated calling of Mitsuyo are the household bustle itself.
- R19 — Zenpei's garbled echo of the allotment-money terms is his incredulous repetition of Tatsuya's proposal in mid-negotiation; recasting it as a tidy direct question would rationalise the procedural talk the reading asks to keep airless.
- R20 as a textual change — the closing fragments and the unstated 'it' already stand as written; the disagreement with F5 is recorded below instead.

Disagreements and unsettled points:
- p14 (F1 against R9's span, though they pull together): faithful — 国色 is the daughter alone; readable — 'in his breast' is not English. Choice: both points taken in one line, 'she a peerless beauty' and 'to himself'. The reading settles it; not sent up.
- p28 (R12): faithful — Zenpei's threefold 'lies' must echo Mitsuyo's 'truly' unvaried; readable — English cannot laugh a lie. Choice: 'shall I laugh in lies, lies, lies?', keeping the repetition and giving the verb an object it can govern. Settled by the repetition motif; not sent up.
- p48 (R14): faithful — 朝飯前 is Tatsuya's brisk sporting idiom and must stay visible; readable — 'as easy as breakfast' alone is a calque. Choice: the idiom kept, hyphen supplied, explanatory expansion declined. The soliloquy's untroubled sporting voice settles it; not sent up.
- p132 (F5 against R20): faithful — 明日は誰が身の is a hanging fragment and 'shall it fall' completes it; readable — a bare fragment reads as dropped words, not withholding. Choice: the present 'Tomorrow, upon whom shall it fall' stands, with what falls still unnamed. The reading demands the withholding but does not settle whether English may supply the verb, and the final line is where being wrong matters most — sent up to the editor.
- p77-p78 (F4): the source prints 鋼雄 twice for 綱雄. Choice: English keeps 'Tsunao' and the variant is flagged, not silently absorbed — sent up for a check against the 1895 text.

Nothing in this part showed that an earlier part should be re-read: who anyone is and what the repeated words mean here match the house's understanding, apart from the name-variant flag above.

House log: The desk took the readers' corrections on the beauty's reference, the introduction at p43, the consistent 'Uncle', Zenpei's laughter, the rank-title and the closing catalogue of the mine, while refusing every change that would gloss, vary or complete what the text deliberately leaves strange, repeated or unresolved.
